title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
text:
Ecological & Conservation Context
    
    
      Satellite telemetry and marine ecological research: feeding aggregations, transboundary migrations, and conservation priorities.

title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
text:
Important Habitats

Tracking Observation: Tagged sharks and sightings clustered at Wreck Bay (12.1°S–12.2°S) during austral summer (November–February), dominated by immature and subadult males.
Scientific Interpretation: Wreck Bay is eastern Australia’s first confirmed aggregation site, where young sharks assemble to exploit seasonal coral and fish spawning prey pulses for growth.


  🔬 Scientific Details: Diving & Surface Thermoregulation
  
    
      Whale sharks dive into deep, cold water (>1,000 m) to forage, returning to the warm surface mixed layer to bask ("behavioral thermoregulation"), which exposes fin-mounted tags to transmit satellite uplinks.

title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
text:
International Movements

Tracking Observation: Satellite tracks crossed international boundaries and deep ocean basins, including Ali traveling ~11,378 km into Papua New Guinea waters and GBR1 reaching 6.3°S in the Solomon Sea.
Scientific Interpretation: Whale sharks operate on oceanic scales beyond national borders, requiring continuous migratory corridors across geopolitical jurisdictions.


  🌐 Scientific Details: Jurisdictional Gaps & International Treaties
  
    
      Jurisdictional Disconnect: Sharks protected inside Australian marine parks lose legal protection when entering unmanaged high seas or foreign waters.
      Multilateral Treaties: Transboundary movements require international cooperation under CMS Appendix I/II (protecting migratory ranges) and CITES Appendix II (regulating trade).

title: Whale Shark Ecology & Conservation in the Coral Sea
text:
Conservation

Tracking Observation: Telemetry pinpoints predictable seasonal aggregation timing, surface residency zones, and open-ocean migratory corridors.
Scientific Interpretation: For an Endangered species with >50% global decline, tracking data enables targeted marine park zoning, vessel speed restrictions, and eco-tourism guidelines.


  ⚠️ Scientific Details: Key Anthropogenic Threats
  
    
      Vessel Strikes: Surface swimming and basking in shipping lanes make whale sharks vulnerable to commercial ship collisions.
      Bycatch & Fishing Gear: Tuna schools aggregate beneath whale sharks, risking entanglement in purse-seine nets and ghost gear.
      Disturbance & Climate Shifts: Shipping noise and diver crowding disrupt habitats, while warming seas alter plankton bloom timing.

title: Profiles of Individual Whale Sharks Tracked
text:
Individual Profiles & Demographics
    
    
      2,391 whale shark (Rhincodon typus) observations in Australia's Coral Sea: 2,255 satellite transmissions from 18 named sharks along the Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea reefs with 136 opportunistic sightings recorded from 2007 to 2018.

  Megashark (Tag ID: 252324)
  
    Male · Immature
    423 Transmissions
    Span: 13.0 Months (2023-11-30 to 2024-12-31)
    Min. Distance: ~6,073 km
    Latitudes: 16.5°S to 9.7°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Forms the tallest trajectory on the scatter plot (reaching 423 cumulative detections). After climbing steeply over its first few summer months, it flattens across a 49-day mid-year gap before surging strongly again between Months 10 and 13.
    Ecological Takeaway: Shows classic seasonal cycling — frequent surface foraging during back-to-back austral summers separated by deeper offshore winter roaming across more than 6,000 km of the Coral Sea.
  



  Alexios (Tag ID: 178953)
  
    Male · Immature
    357 Transmissions
    Span: 5.2 Months (2021-12-05 to 2022-05-12)
    Min. Distance: ~4,307 km
    Latitudes: 18.1°S to 11.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Rises rapidly and smoothly to 357 detections in just over 5 months (~2.3 transmissions/day) with no silent gap longer than 13 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: Indicates sustained surface and upper-water-column activity as this immature male traveled over 4,300 km along the outer Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea basin from summer into autumn.
  



  Ali (Tag ID: 178954)
  
    Female · Immature
    273 Transmissions
    Span: 25.3 Months (2021-12-06 to 2024-01-15)
    Min. Distance: ~11,378 km
    Latitudes: 18.6°S to 7.9°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Stretches farthest right among all tagged sharks (25.3 months / >2 years), advancing in staircase-like seasonal bursts separated by gaps of up to 73 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: One of only two confirmed females in the tagged cohort and the dataset's long-distance marathoner, logging over 11,300 km between central Queensland latitudes and waters near Papua New Guinea.
  



  Sharpie (Tag ID: 252325)
  
    Male · Immature
    261 Transmissions
    Span: 3.2 Months (2023-12-01 to 2024-03-07)
    Min. Distance: ~1,544 km
    Latitudes: 13.5°S to 11.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: One of the steepest initial slopes on the chart, packing 261 locations into 97 days (~2.7 uplinks/day) with a maximum gap of only 10 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: Stayed within a relatively tight northern reef band (11.3°S–13.5°S), spending long periods basking and filter-feeding at the surface during peak summer plankton productivity.
  



  Juanita (Tag ID: 172900)
  
    Unknown Sex · Immature
    204 Transmissions
    Span: 4.3 Months (2023-11-03 to 2024-03-14)
    Min. Distance: ~2,642 km
    Latitudes: 16.6°S to 8.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Climbs steadily from Month 0 to 204 detections across 4.3 months, punctuated by brief 1–3 week pauses (max gap 21 days).
    Ecological Takeaway: Tracked earlier in spring (early November) than most sharks and ranged widely across 8.5 degrees of latitude northward into the northern Coral Sea.
  



  GBR1 (Tag ID: 172899)
  
    Unknown Sex · Immature
    177 Transmissions
    Span: 4.8 Months (2018-10-26 to 2019-03-21)
    Min. Distance: ~3,677 km
    Latitudes: 14.2°S to 6.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Exceptionally smooth, unbroken upward line over nearly 5 months — never going more than 4 days without a satellite uplink.
    Ecological Takeaway: Reached the northernmost latitude of any shark in the dataset (6.3°S in Papua New Guinea waters), proving cross-border movement across the northern Coral Sea.
  



  Beizam (Tag ID: 243952)
  
    Male · Subadult
    98 Transmissions
    Span: 2.2 Months (2023-12-02 to 2024-02-08)
    Min. Distance: ~1,846 km
    Latitudes: 17.2°S to 11.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Steady 2.2-month climb to 98 detections across December–February with minimal transmission gaps.
    Ecological Takeaway: Notable as the only Subadult shark in an otherwise immature-dominated tagged group, cruising rapidly southward and offshore (~27 km/day) across nearly 6 degrees of latitude.
  



  Blancpain (Tag ID: 178957)
  
    Female · Immature
    73 Transmissions
    Span: 17.3 Months (2021-12-06 to 2023-05-16)
    Min. Distance: ~1,943 km
    Latitudes: 14.5°S to 8.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Features the most dramatic horizontal plateau on the entire plot — going silent for 276 consecutive days (~9 months) before resuming transmissions past Month 15.
    Ecological Takeaway: Along with Ali, one of only two tagged females; demonstrates how whale sharks can spend months foraging in deep or remote waters without long surface intervals before reappearing the next season.
  



  GBR2 (Tag ID: 176413)
  
    Male · Immature
    69 Transmissions
    Span: 2.9 Months (2019-11-17 to 2020-02-13)
    Min. Distance: ~2,675 km
    Latitudes: 15.1°S to 10.8°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Moderate 3-month summer curve reaching 69 uplinks with occasional 1–2 week diving gaps.
    Ecological Takeaway: Covered high daily mileage (~30 km/day average between pings), moving briskly across outer Coral Sea reefs during the 2019–2020 summer season.
  



  Infamis (Tag ID: 243954)
  
    Male · Immature
    66 Transmissions
    Span: 2.4 Months (2023-12-01 to 2024-02-12)
    Min. Distance: ~644 km
    Latitudes: 13.8°S to 12.2°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Compact 2.4-month summer trajectory rising to 66 detections near the base of the main summer cluster.
    Ecological Takeaway: Showed strong site fidelity within a narrow 1.6° latitude band along the northern Great Barrier Reef shelf edge rather than making an immediate long-distance crossing.
  



  Jaap (Tag ID: 178948)
  
    Male · Immature
    63 Transmissions
    Span: 1.3 Months (2019-11-19 to 2019-12-28)
    Min. Distance: ~255 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 11.6°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Steep short-duration curve reaching 63 locations within 39 days (~1.6 uplinks/day).
    Ecological Takeaway: Remained tightly localized around the Wreck Bay / northern reef aggregation hotspot during late November and December coral spawning.
  



  Halliday (Tag ID: 243955)
  
    Male · Immature
    53 Transmissions
    Span: 1.3 Months (2023-12-04 to 2024-01-12)
    Min. Distance: ~772 km
    Latitudes: 15.0°S to 11.3°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Climbs cleanly to 53 detections over 39 days across December and early January.
    Ecological Takeaway: Unlike Jaap over the same 39-day span, Halliday traveled more than three times farther (~772 km), heading southward along the outer reef margin.
  



  Hugh (Tag ID: 243951)
  
    Male · Immature
    53 Transmissions
    Span: 0.2 Months / 7 Days (2023-11-30 to 2023-12-07)
    Min. Distance: ~143 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 12.0°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Appears nearly vertical near Month 0, recording 53 high-frequency transmissions in just one week (~7.6 uplinks/day!).
    Ecological Takeaway: Captures intense, continuous surface feeding right after tagging before the tag ceased reporting or detached.
  



  Fifty_Fathoms (Tag ID: 178951)
  
    Male · Immature
    24 Transmissions
    Span: 1.2 Months (2021-12-05 to 2022-01-11)
    Min. Distance: ~868 km
    Latitudes: 14.6°S to 11.5°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Low, gentle 1.2-month curve reaching 24 transmissions over 37 days.
    Ecological Takeaway: Despite fewer surface uplinks, covered nearly 870 km across 3 degrees of latitude — suggesting deeper travel with briefer surface intervals.
  



  Sapphire (Tag ID: 176409)
  
    Male · Immature
    24 Transmissions
    Span: 0.3 Months / 9 Days (2024-03-05 to 2024-03-14)
    Min. Distance: ~1,387 km
    Latitudes: 16.5°S to 12.7°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Short 9-day burst of 24 detections near the origin of the X-axis.
    Ecological Takeaway: Tracked in March (late summer/early autumn) rather than December, moving rapidly across wide Coral Sea distances in just over a week.
  



  Andrew (Tag ID: 243953)
  
    Male · Immature
    18 Transmissions
    Span: 0.2 Months / 5 Days (2023-12-01 to 2023-12-06)
    Min. Distance: ~76 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 11.9°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Brief 5-day cluster of 18 transmissions right at Month 0.
    Ecological Takeaway: Represents short-term local foraging around the northern reef tagging site in early December before early tag loss or deep offshore departure.
  



  Dotti (Tag ID: 178949)
  
    Male · Immature
    10 Transmissions
    Span: 0.1 Months / 3 Days (2019-11-20 to 2019-11-23)
    Min. Distance: ~20 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Compact 10-point cluster at the bottom-left origin of the plot.
    Ecological Takeaway: Captures a 3-day snapshot of localized reef aggregation behavior at 12.2°S during the November 2019 tagging expedition.
  



  Ambitious (Tag ID: 176407)
  
    Unknown Sex · Immature
    9 Transmissions
    Span: 0.2 Months / 6 Days (2019-11-19 to 2019-11-25)
    Min. Distance: ~19 km
    Latitudes: 12.2°S to 12.1°S
  
  
    Curve Pattern on Plot: Shortest tagged trajectory on the graph (9 uplinks across 6 days near Month 0).
    Ecological Takeaway: Like Dotti, illustrates both localized reef feeding at 12.2°S and a real-world challenge of marine telemetry — tags can shed early or stop reporting once a shark dives into deep water.

title: About This Project
section: Why Were the Whale Sharks Tracked?
text:
Why Were the Whale Sharks Tracked?
Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) are globally Endangered. Researchers combined citizen-science sightings (2007–2024, via Sharkbook and Eye on the Reef) with satellite tags on 18 individual sharks (2018–2023) to answer key conservation questions:

Mapping Hidden Migrations: Satellite telemetry reveals whether sharks stay on local reefs year-round or roam across deep ocean basins toward Papua New Guinea and the wider Indo-Pacific.
Guiding Marine Protection: Tracking where sharks surface helps pinpoint overlaps with shipping lanes, fishing activity, and protected zones inside the Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea Marine Parks.

      🧭 How to Read This Map
    
  
  
  
    Key guideposts for interpreting the data:
  

  
    
      📍 Sightings vs. Satellite Tracks
      Historical sightings (coral markers) represent opportunistic observations from 2007–2018. Satellite tracking records (teal markers) represent locations transmitted by satellite tags attached to 18 individual sharks between 2018 and 2024.
    

    
      👥 Markers vs. Population Size
      Multiple markers clustered in one location indicate repeated observations over time, not a larger population gathering at once.
    

    
      📡 Why Tracking Gaps Occur
      Satellite tags only uplink when a shark surfaces. Gaps between points mean the shark was swimming submerged or diving, not that it stopped moving.
    

    
      🔥 Heatmaps & Observation Density
      Heatmaps highlight concentrations of recorded points and tagging effort, not whale shark population density.
    
  

  
    Map Legend:

      Synthesis & Ecological Insights
    
    
      What the Data Tells Us
    
    
      Three key behavioral, seasonal, and geographic patterns identified from 18 satellite tracking trajectories and 136 opportunistic sighting records in the Coral Sea.
    
  

  

    
    
      
        
        
          🌐 Pattern 1 · Spatial Scale
        
        
      

      
        Long-Distance Movements

        
          What the Data Shows:
          Individual whale sharks traveled thousands of kilometers across the open Coral Sea rather than remaining tied to a single local reef:
          
            Ali: Tracked across 25.3 months, traveling a recorded minimum of ~11,378 km between central Queensland and Papua New Guinea (18.6°S to 7.9°S).
            Megashark: Covered ~6,073 km over 13.0 months, ranging between 16.5°S and 9.7°S.
            Alexios: Logged ~4,307 km in 5.2 months along outer reef edges.
          
        

        
          Ecological Meaning:
          Whale sharks move well beyond individual reef systems, routinely navigating deep ocean basins and crossing international maritime boundaries.
        
      
    

    
    
      
        
        
          ☀️ Pattern 2 · Seasonal Timing
        
        
      

      
        Seasonal Movement Patterns

        
          What the Data Shows:
          Satellite transmission records cluster from November through February, followed by sharp drops during winter months (May–September).
        

        
          Possible Ecological Explanations:
          Summer conditions, nutrient upwelling, and coral and fish spawning generate dense plankton blooms, attracting whale sharks to the surface to forage.
        

        
          ⚠️ Scientific Distinction: Satellite tags only record surface uplinks. Frequent transmissions indicate surface presence, but surface activity alone does not prove active feeding behavior.
        
      
    

    
    
      
        
        
          📍 Pattern 3 · Key Habitat
        
        
      

      
        Geographic Patterns & Wreck Bay

        
          What the Data Shows:
          Records reveal a pronounced cluster centered on Wreck Bay (12.1°S–12.2°S) along the outer shelf of the far northern Great Barrier Reef, eastern Australia's primary confirmed aggregation hub.
        

        
          Conservation Importance:
          Only about 30 whale shark aggregation sites are known globally. Identifying aggregation hubs like Wreck Bay allows authorities to establish seasonal protection zones, manage shipping traffic, and minimize accidental fishing interactions.

    Scientific Rigor & Context
    Limitations of the Research
    
      Understanding what telemetry data reveals and where uncertainties remain is essential for sound conservation science.
    
  

  
    
    
      🦈
      
        Sample Size
        
          Eighteen tagged individuals may not reflect the movement patterns, age classes, or sex ratios of the entire Coral Sea population.
        
      
    

    
    
      📡
      
        Tracking Gaps
        
          Tags transmit only at the surface; transmission gaps reflect deep diving or foraging, not shark absence.
        
      
    

    
    
      📍
      
        Sighting Bias
        
          Historical sightings cluster where people regularly visit (dive and tourism hubs), reflecting human observation effort.
        
      
    

    
    
      🏊
      
        Behavioral Context
        
          Satellite coordinates record location and surface basking, but do not directly confirm feeding, resting, or mating.
        
      
    

    
    
      🌏
      
        Geographic Scope
        
          Findings reflect Coral Sea and southwest Pacific oceanography, rather than all global whale shark populations.
        
      
    

    
    
      🏷️
      
        Tag Retention
        
          Attachment retention, battery lifespan, and satellite pass timing create differences in tracking duration across sharks.
        
      
    
  

  
    💡 Why Limitations Matter
    
      Recognizing data limits prevents overgeneralization and ensures marine protection measures are founded on solid evidence.
